items.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996
items.q: I met him in New York and we became friends... I went in for a month with him... Junior Mance went with Dinah for a while... And you’ve been working with Junior Mance recently? Yeah. On the cruise things.

ctx.x: I met him in New York and we became friends or something. And I left Dinah at one time, and he was going into the Cafe Bohemia, and he said, “well come on in, I’m going in for a month.” And I said okay. And I went in for a month with him and it was Cannon, Nat, Junior Mance and Specks Wright out of Philadelphia, and myself. And then I went back to Washington, I had to go back to Washington, and so he said, “well can you recommend a bass player?” And I said well a good friend of mine is Sam Jones, try and get him,…
I think it’s really fascinating how musicians recommend each other and they move around from group to group.

items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Keter Betts is the bass player... we were put together as a trio on the cruise... the three of us played

ctx.x: Is there a story behind this piece? The way you sat down —

No. Not really. I didn’t know what to call it, and then “Harlem Lullaby” stuck. But believe it or not I just recorded it again and I did it on this live session. And the producer liked it so well that I just did a record for them a few months ago. It should be out either this month or next month. And he asked me would I do it again for the session, I mean in the studio, and I did it. And I would have to send you that one because you know after you’ve done a tune a lot, then sometimes it either gets better or…

session. For one thing, recording for Enja, this particular producer I had, Horst Weber out of Munich, he insists on any, even in the studio, it’s almost like doing a live date because he will only use first takes. And just by coincidence he has the same idea about recording, which is, when you’ve got to do two or three takes, and I’ve always had this idea, if I have to repeat a thing, it goes downhill. Usually the first take, you’ve got the feeling that you want. You may miss a few notes. Horst doesn’t care. He…
